To outgross something or someone means to earn more money in total revenue than another thing or person, typically in a competition or comparison.

The key word buried inside it is "gross," which in financial language simply means the total amount of money earned before any expenses, taxes, or deductions are taken out. Think of it as the raw, full number on the scoreboard — every dollar that came in, counted together.

The prefix "out-" means to beat, surpass, or do better than someone else in a specific way. You already know this from everyday words like outrun (run faster than), outsmart (be smarter than), or outlast (last longer than).

So put them together: outgross = to earn a higher gross revenue than someone or something else.

This word appears most heavily in the film and entertainment industry, where movies are constantly being compared by how much money they made at the box office (the total ticket sales worldwide or domestically).

"Avatar outgrossed Titanic to become the highest-earning film of all time."

This means Avatar pulled in more total ticket revenue than Titanic did.

"The sequel outgrossed the original by nearly $200 million."

The sequel earned $200 million more in total than the first film.

You'll also see it in business and finance more broadly:

"Company A outgrossed Company B in the second quarter."

Company A brought in more total revenue than Company B during that period.

Imagine two lemonade stands in your neighborhood. At the end of the week, Stand A collected $300 in sales and Stand B collected $180.

Stand A outgrossed Stand B. It doesn't matter what they spent on lemons, cups, or sugar — those are expenses, and gross doesn't care about expenses. Gross is only about what came in. Stand A simply brought in more money.

1. Gross ≠ Profit.
This is critical. Outgrossing something does not automatically mean being more profitable. A film can outgross another film in ticket sales and still lose money if it cost far more to make. Outgross is purely about the top-line number — total revenue collected — not what's left over after costs.

Example: Film X earned $500 million (cost $450 million to make). Film Y earned $300 million (cost $80 million to make). Film X outgrossed Film Y — but Film Y was actually more profitable.

2. The comparison is always relative.
You always outgross something — a rival, a predecessor, a record. The word implies a head-to-head comparison. You wouldn't say "this film outgrossed" and stop there; it needs an opponent or a benchmark to beat.

3. It's a transitive verb.
This means it always needs an object — something being outgrossed. You outgross a film, a competitor, a record, a rival company.

ConceptExplanation

Outgross means to exceed another entity in gross (total) earnings. It's used when comparing revenue figures between two things — usually films, companies, or products. It says nothing about profit, only about which one brought in more money altogether. The winner of that comparison is said to have outgrossed the other.
